utterances.speaker: host
utterances.text: At CES 2026, the headline isn’t one new phone or TV. It’s the industry’s pivot toward AI infrastructure and robotics—what some are calling “physical AI,” where systems perceive, decide, and act in the real world. The show floor is increasingly about chips, sensors, and platforms that make autonomy and robots scalable.

utterances.speaker: expert
utterances.text: That term, physical AI, is basically AI with a body—or at least AI that can control machines safely and reliably. It’s why you’re seeing more emphasis on edge computing, power efficiency, and real-time performance rather than just consumer features. CES is reflecting a shift from demos to deployment.

utterances.speaker: host
utterances.text: Give us a few examples of what “deployment” looks like this year. What stood out as proof that companies are building the plumbing, not just the prototypes?

utterances.speaker: expert
utterances.text: On the vehicle side, NVIDIA’s DRIVE Thor showed up in a Level 4 robotaxi context with WeRide, which signals the stack is maturing beyond test tracks. On the robotics side, NVIDIA’s Jetson Thor is positioned as a scalable compute platform for machines that need fast perception and control. And Tesla talked about its Arm-based AI5 chip, claiming a big jump in performance over the prior generation, which is part of the same trend: more compute closer to where decisions happen.

utterances.speaker: host
utterances.text: Humanoid robots are also back in a big way at CES, but the pitch sounds different now. It’s less “look what it can do,” and more “here’s where it will work.” What’s driving that change?

utterances.speaker: expert
utterances.text: Two things: capability and economics. Boston Dynamics’ Atlas, for example, is being framed around industrial use, with plans tied to Hyundai plants and an ambition for large-scale manufacturing down the line. Meanwhile, companies like AgiBot and others are emphasizing modular lineups and real deployments in manufacturing and retail, which suggests the business case is becoming clearer.

utterances.speaker: host
utterances.text: So it’s not just humanoids, it’s an ecosystem: chips, cloud integrations, and even digital twins to speed up production. And there’s also the policy layer—because autonomy and wearables raise new questions. What are you hearing from the people who track the industry?

utterances.speaker: expert
utterances.text: Industry voices at CES, including leaders from the Consumer Technology Association, are describing a clear arc from simple home robots—like vacuums—to more functional machines that can operate in complex spaces. There’s also a lot of attention on infrastructure sessions, including AI and even quantum discussions, because the bottleneck is increasingly compute, power, and reliability. And as autonomy expands, regulation becomes a practical constraint, not an abstract debate.
